questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A fit figure and a forecasting figure that disagree
questions.learningObjective: interpret a large gap between in-sample and out-of-sample error
questions.stem: A model's root mean squared error on the data it was fitted to is 2.1, and its mean absolute error across rolling origins is 8.4, four times larger. What does this support?

options.text: That the fit is much better than the forecasting, since a model with enough flexibility can reproduce structure specific to the observations it was given and none of it is available on a period it has not seen
That the two figures measure different things and neither is wrong, so a ratio of four between them is unremarkable and needs no explanation
options.misconception: dismisses a fourfold gap as a matter of units

options.text: That the rolling origins were chosen badly, since a fourfold increase in error is too large to be caused by a data sample alone
options.misconception: blames the evaluation design for the gap

options.text: That the model is well specified but under-trained, since more data would close a gap of this size without any change to its form
options.misconception: assumes a large gap is a data volume problem

questions.explanation: A fourfold gap between the two figures is the measurement, and it is the classic symptom of a model that has fitted the sample rather than the process. Two measures are being compared rather than one, which is true and does not make the ratio unremarkable: the two are on similar scales and the gap is large enough that it would be remarkable if it were nothing. The distinction between fitting and forecasting is not a technicality here, because a flexible specification will absorb noise, and the noise it absorbs is not repeatable. More data of the same kind would close some of the gap by making the sample-specific component a smaller share of the total, which is a real and useful effect, and it would not close the whole of it, because a model with too many terms for the structure present will keep finding things to fit on a larger sample as well.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two figures the model was allowed to see while it was being built.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An interval that covers less than it promises on the periods that matter
questions.learningObjective: test an interval claim against the periods on which it was checked
questions.stem: A 90 per cent interval is published for a monthly series. Over 200 rolling origins it covered the outcome 183 times overall, and it covered 61 of the 66 origins that fell in the third quarter of the year, against 122 of 134 in the other three quarters. What does this support?

options.text: That the overall 0.915 is flattered by the other quarters, since the third quarter covers 0.924 of its origins with no visible shortfall and the pooled figure conceals a difference worth examining
That the interval meets its 90 per cent promise, since 183 out of 200 is above 0.90 and the promise is a statement about the whole series
options.misconception: accepts a pooled figure as settling a per-season question

options.text: That the third quarter is a small enough slice to ignore, since 66 origins out of 200 cannot support a claim about one quarter on its own
options.misconception: dismisses a slice for being small rather than testing it

options.text: That the interval is too wide in the other three quarters, since 122 of 134 indicates a level of caution that the third quarter does not need
options.misconception: reads a high coverage rate as over-wide

questions.explanation: The pooled figure is 0.915 against a promise of 0.90, and the pooled figure is the one that goes in the report, which is exactly why the breakdown is worth computing. The quarterly rates are 0.924 and 0.910, and the difference between them is a handful of origins, so the honest conclusion is that this table has not established that the interval behaves differently by season. What the breakdown does buy is the ability to say that, rather than leaving a reader to assume the pooled number describes every season equally, and a difference of this size is exactly the kind that becomes obvious once a real structural change appears and is invisible in the average. A claim about one quarter needs enough origins to support it, and 66 is few, which is a reason to keep collecting rather than a reason to stop looking.
questions.hint: Compute the rate within each slice, and ask what the pooled rate is averaging over.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which model and which stated limit belong together
questions.learningObjective: pair a forecast method with the limitation its claim should state
questions.stem: A supplier offers a smoothed forecast for a weekly series and a claim attached to it. Two pairings of method and stated limit are on the table. Which pairing survives scrutiny?

options.text: A smoothed forecast with the limit that it carries no seasonal state, so the claim should name the cycles it cannot represent and a seasonal method as the alternative
A smoothed forecast with the limit that it is only valid for a single period ahead, so the claim should say the horizon may not be extended beyond the next observation
options.misconception: restricts the horizon rather than naming the missing state

options.text: A seasonal method with the limit that it needs a full cycle of history, so the claim should name the warm-up the model requires before its forecasts mean anything
options.misconception: states a real limit against the wrong method

options.text: A seasonal method with the limit that its interval is approximate, so the claim should present the coverage as indicative rather than measured
options.misconception: hedges a coverage figure instead of measuring it

questions.explanation: A stated limit is useful when it names the structure the method does not represent, because that tells a reader which alternative to look at. A method carrying only a level and a trend state has nowhere to put a repeating pattern, and on a seasonal series it will smooth the cycle away and forecast a level that is wrong by the size of the swing in every season, which is a structural omission rather than a matter of tuning. The second option describes a real property of smoothed forecasts, that they are most trustworthy one step out, and states it as though it were a horizon restriction rather than as the consequence of carrying no seasonal state. The third and fourth pair honest observations with the wrong method, and the fourth is the weakest because a coverage figure that is described as indicative rather than measured has simply not been computed.
questions.hint: Ask what state the method has available, and therefore which structures it cannot carry.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a walk-forward evaluation does and does not establish
questions.learningObjective: explain what a walk-forward evaluation establishes about a forecast method
questions.stem: Explain what a walk-forward evaluation of a forecast method does and does not establish, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: A walk-forward evaluation establishes that the method, refitted as it would be in production and asked only for forecasts it could actually have made at each origin, has produced errors of a stated size on a stated series over a stated period, and that is a real and much stronger claim than an in-sample figure because every forecast was made before its outcome was known. What it does not establish is that the errors will continue at that size, that the method will do as well on a series it was not developed against, or that a smaller average error corresponds to a better decision, which is a claim about the loss the errors cause rather than about their magnitude. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the method achieves an average error of 4.2, so it is suitable for planning. A number is not a suitability finding, and the gap between the two is where a forecast programme either earns trust or spends it, since an average error that was measured on a calm period says very little about the period a plan is actually built for. A second wrong sentence says the evaluation proves the model is right, when what it produces is evidence of a size, gathered by a method whose own design deserves to be stated.

questions.explanation: The value of the walk-forward design is that it removes the one thing an in-sample figure cannot, which is the model's access to its own future. What remains uncertain is everything about the conditions, and the honest report says which conditions held. Reporting the distribution of errors beside the average, and reporting them by horizon, keeps the parts that a pooled number discards in view.
questions.hint: Ask what the evaluation had access to at each origin, and what the resulting number is a statement about.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a seasonal index is and is not claiming
questions.learningObjective: explain what a seasonal index asserts and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Explain what a seasonal index asserts about a series, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: A seasonal index asserts that the same positions in the cycle behave alike across cycles, so that the average behaviour of a position can stand in for its behaviour in the cycle now being forecast, and that the positions can be separated from the level without either one absorbing the other. The second half of that claim is the one usually forgotten, and it is what the zero-sum constraint on an additive profile and the average-to-one constraint on a multiplicative one are for. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the index gives the exact effect of the season, so the forecast error is the rest. The index is an average over past cycles, so it carries the variation between cycles inside it and cannot be treated as a known quantity to be removed, and the variation it leaves behind is real error rather than a residual of the calculation. A second wrong sentence treats the index as permanent, which turns a summary of the past into a promise about the future, and it is the sentence behind a forecast that was never updated after the season it described had changed.

questions.explanation: An index is a parameter estimated from data, and every property of an estimate applies to it, including the one that matters most here, which is that it was estimated on a sample of cycles. Reporting the index alongside the number of cycles behind it and the spread across them turns a bare number into something a reader can weigh, and it is the cheapest improvement available to a seasonal forecast.
questions.hint: Ask how many cycles the index is an average of, and what happens to the variation between them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the horizon changes which method is wanted
questions.learningObjective: explain why a longer horizon calls for a different forecast structure
questions.stem: Explain why the length of a forecast horizon changes which structure a forecast should have, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: The horizon changes which parts of the series a forecast can still lean on, and it changes them at different rates. At one step the last observation is nearly all of the information available, so a forecast that carries a level and updates it on the new observation is close to optimal. At thirty steps the series has moved on thirty times, the last observation has said much less about where the process now is, and the only things still carrying information are the slower structures: a trend, a seasonal profile, and whatever the level has been converging to. That is why a method tuned on a short horizon is a poor choice for a long one, and why the method and the horizon have to be chosen together rather than the horizon being a parameter passed in afterwards. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the same model serves every horizon, so only the error grows with distance. The structure is what has to change, not merely the width of the interval around it, and a model with no trend state extrapolates a flat line a month ahead with some confidence and a year ahead with none at all, however the interval is scaled.

questions.explanation: The variance of the forecast error growing with the horizon is universal and is not the point. The point is that the sources of predictability differ by horizon, so the relative value of a trend state or a seasonal state changes as the distance does, and a method is being asked to do different jobs at different distances. Choosing per horizon, and reporting which method was used at each, is the arrangement that follows.
questions.hint: Ask what information survives at thirty steps that did not matter at one, and which state the method carries.
